source.title: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups
source.authors: Davide Ghilardi; Federico Belotti; Marco Molinari

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures SAE reconstruction error and the downstream effect of replacing activations with SAE reconstructions, but does not test the claim’s linear predictability, token-level scaling, or error structure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports FVU and next-token cross-entropy changes for grouped and smaller SAEs. The cross-entropy measure tests the effect of SAE reconstruction, but there is no comparison with random errors of the same size. It does not measure token-level error norms, predictability from input activations, or whether different SAE sizes fail on the same contexts.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes Group-SAE, one SAE per group of similar layers, as a way to cut training cost. Every result compares its own method with per-layer, evenly spaced or smaller SAEs on aggregate FVU, ΔCE and auto-interpretability. It never measures the structure of SAE error: no linear prediction of the error from the input (V1), no per-token error norms across SAE sizes (V2), no random-error control of equal size (V3), no linear/nonlinear split (V4), no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term (V5), and no test of whether dark matter is a training artifact (V6). It does not cite or use the dark-matter paper. The relation is set to cites_only only because no closer option fits.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that grouping contiguous layers by angular distance cuts SAE training cost by up to about 50% (42.5–53.7% in Table 2), with only a slight loss in reconstruction and comparable downstream and interpretability results. They also find AMAD-based grouping beats evenly spaced groups and smaller per-layer SAEs at equal compute, except on one metric for Pythia-160M. They draw no conclusions about SAE error structure.
record.recipe_differences: The study groups model layers to share SAEs and evaluates aggregate FVU and downstream cross-entropy changes; it does not investigate dark-matter predictability or compare SAE errors with matched random errors.
record.method_sensitivity: Reconstruction and downstream metrics worsen as AMAD increases and the number of groups decreases; the authors identify a turning point around AMAD(G) ≈ 0.2.

fits_no_version.finding: In the tested Pythia models, Group-SAEs chosen by AMAD<0.2 give slightly lower FVU and ΔCE than smaller per-layer SAEs at matched FLOPs. Compared with full per-layer SAEs they cost about 0.015 FVU and 0.6 points of ΔCE while saving roughly 42–54% of compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs shared across groups of angularly similar layers keep reconstruction and downstream fidelity close to per-layer SAEs at much lower training cost.

record.problems: No matched random-error comparison is reported for the reconstruction-induced cross-entropy change. The error measures reported are aggregated rather than token-level; the tested models and SAE setup are limited to Pythia models, TopK activation, and expansion factor 16. Standard deviations are shown in figures, but Table 1 reports no uncertainty values.
record.rows_left_out: No separately plotted per-group or per-G results were extracted; Figure 2 and Figure 3 show sweeps over configurations but do not provide tabulated values for each point.

untested.parts: All: no linear probe of the SAE error from the input activations.
All: one expansion factor (16), no per-token error norms, no context-overlap analysis across sizes.
All: ΔCE is reported without a random-error comparison of equal norm.
All: no circuit or steering analysis.
All: only TopK with a fixed setup; no comparison of architectures or objectives on error structure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification and the V3 links are wrong. Nonzero ΔCE alone does not test V3, which needs a comparison against random errors of equal norm. All rows are comparisons of the study's own method against baselines.

versions.untested_parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from input activations.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap in contexts where larger and smaller SAEs fail, and whether error persists with scale.
The paper measures loss change after SAE reconstruction, but does not compare it with random errors of the same size.
Whether the linear component represents unlearned features and whether the nonlinear component resists further dictionary learning.
Whether SAE-feature-based circuits or steering lose behavior when the error term is omitted.
Whether dark matter is mainly a training artifact or shrinks with alternative architectures or end-to-end training.

relation.reason: The text discusses general SAE reconstruction and efficiency and cites related SAE work, but contains no identifiable citation or attribution of the dark-matter finding. Its connection is contextual discussion, without a test or use of the claim.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates layer grouping through aggregate reconstruction, downstream loss and interpretability metrics. It neither tests nor uses any of V1–V6; reconstruction patching lacks the matched random-error control required by V3.

source_check.notes: All twelve rows accurately report method-comparison results, but should not serve as phenomenon evidence under verdict_rules.md section 2. The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated 20 September 2025, despite the record's 2024 year.
